draft_context.source_title: The hottest indie game on Steam just had a malware scare
draft_context.description: A malicious Meccha Chameleon Steam Workshop map was found attempting to download malware onto players' PCs. Here's what happened, why it matters, and how to stay safe.
paragraphs: One of Steam’s biggest success stories of 2026 has suddenly found itself at the center of a security scare. A security researcher has discovered that a community-made Meccha Chameleon Workshop map contained code designed to write files outside the game and launch a hidden PowerShell process that attempted to download an additional payload from an external server.

The investigation, published by security researcher Feint , began after players noticed a Command Prompt window briefly flashing on screen while Steam downloaded a custom Workshop map called Laser Tag Neon. Digging deeper, the researcher found that the map wasn’t hiding an executable file in the traditional sense. Instead, it abused Unreal Engine 5 Blueprint logic to write a batch file into the user’s Documents folder before launching a hidden PowerShell process.

Laser Tag Neon on Steam (now unavailable) Steam Community According to the reverse engineering analysis, the script then attempted to download a second-stage batch file from a hardcoded external server and execute it. During testing, however, that download returned a 404 error, meaning the final payload was never retrieved and its intended purpose remains unknown. Even so, the behavior itself — writing executable files outside the game directory and invoking PowerShell — is highly unusual for a Workshop map and strongly suggests malicious intent.

The researcher stopped short of identifying the final malware family because the second-stage payload was unavailable during analysis. However, they concluded that the Workshop item should be treated as malicious based on multiple indicators, including hidden execution logic, disguised Blueprint assets, and attempts to retrieve external code.

Meccha Chameleon isn’t just another indie game. Since launching last month, the multiplayer hit has sold around 15 million copies, and industry analysts recently reported that it generated the second-highest PC game revenue of the month, behind only Fortnite . That massive audience makes it an attractive target for attackers looking to abuse community-created content.

lemorion_1224 Unlike installing a traditional mod manually, Workshop content is often downloaded automatically when joining multiplayer lobbies or subscribing to community maps. In this case, the malicious behavior was embedded inside what appeared to be a perfectly normal Unreal Engine asset, making it difficult to spot through a quick inspection.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The key feature of this Amazon Basics plug is its Matter support. For Apple Home folks, this means you can completely ignore the fact that previous Amazon-branded gear was Alexa only. Because Matter establishes a universal format for smart home hardware, this plug pairs directly with Apple just as easily as it does with Alexa or Google Home. You do not need to download a separate Amazon app just to get it running. As long as you have a Matter-compatible Apple home hub, like a HomePod mini or an Apple TV 4K, the plug talks directly to your existing Apple ecosystem over your Wi-Fi network. There is a Matter code right inside the box

IMO, smart plugs are arguably the most versatile and important building blocks of any smart home setup. While smart bulbs are great for overhead fixtures, outlet adapters let you bring automation to appliances that cannot be easily retrofitted.

Another major win here on this plug is the physical footprint. Early smart plugs were often bulky, frequently blocking both of the outlets and forcing you to use surge protectors. Amazon designed this plug with a highly compact form factor. It fits perfectly into a single socket, leaving the other outlet completely clear for other appliances or a second smart plug if you want to stack them.

There is a trade-off to be aware of before you buy Amazon’s Matter smart plug. This is a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi-only device rather than a Thread-enabled plug. Wi-Fi plugs can occasionally introduce a bit of latency compared to the near-instant response of a Thread device, and they add another device to your router’s legacy client list. However, at a price point under $10, complaining about the lack of Thread is short-sighted. I’ve been using this for the last few weeks, and it’s really solid. It just does what you ask.

draft_context.source_title: SpaceX eyes tower catch for next Starship after auspicious end to 13th flight
draft_context.description: SpaceX was more than lucky Friday, sending its 13th full-scale Starship test flight halfway around the world from South Texas to an on-target, intact splashdown in a remote section of the Indian Ocean. Starship has made precise splashdowns before. This time, however, the ship gently tipped over and came to rest floating in a remote stretch of ocean west of Australia. Previous splashdowns ended with conflagrations, an outcome SpaceX officials have come to expect with each water landing of Starship. The buoyant Starship looked to be in fine shape after reaching the Indian Ocean. SpaceX engineers flew drones over the vehicle to inspect its heat shield, getting their best look yet at how more than 18,000 ceramic tiles insulating the ship's stainless steel airframe weathered the trip to space and back. The tiles withstood temperatures up to 2,600° Fahrenheit (1,430° Celsius) as Starship streaked back into the atmosphere at the end of its hour-long flight from Starbase, Texas. Encouraged by the picture-perfect end to Friday's flight, SpaceX is likely to take the next leap with Starship on the next launch, according to the company's founder and CEO, Elon Musk. That would entail hurling Starship on a longer-range trajectory, perhaps into low-Earth orbit, to bring the vehicle back to the launch site. Mechanical arms on the launch tower will attempt to capture the ship as it slows to a hover. SpaceX has already done this with the rocket's massive Super Heavy booster, which is larger and heavier than Starship itself, but comes back at a fraction of the speed. "Unless we discover problems after mission data review, SpaceX will attempt to catch the ship with the tower on next flight," Musk wrote on X Friday evening. Starship's six Raptor engines afloat in the Indian Ocean. Credit: SpaceX Hungry for data Engineers have long identified the performance and durability of the heat shield as one of the toughest challenges for the Starship program. SpaceX's ambition for Starship includes rapid turnarounds, and eventually multiple flights per day. If this is to be achievable, the heat shield has to be robust against the vibrations and extreme temperatures it sees during launch and reentry. It can't be refurbished or replaced after every flight. "This is the first time we’ve put an intact Starship in the water," said Dan Huot, a SpaceX communications manager providing commentary on the company's live webcast. "This is a dream scenario for the team that’s trying to get this heat shield data." The intact splashdown Friday also opens up the possibility for SpaceX to tow the rocket back to shore, probably somewhere in Australia, for more detailed inspections. Starship is designed for reuse, but not after exposure to salt water. "This is so critical for refining the heat shield and everything else. The really good news is … you’re looking at a pretty intact-looking heat shield," Huot said. "We were flying at a significantly higher dynamic pressure, so putting way more stress on this vehicle on the way uphill, and it's sitting there in the water." SpaceX continued receiving signals from Starship after splashdown through the company's Starlink satellite broadband network. A camera onboard Starship showed no signs of external damage to the vehicle's six Raptor engines as water lapped against the lens. Friday's test flight was the 13th launch of SpaceX's Starship on top of its massive Super Heavy booster, and the second flight of the latest iteration of the world's most powerful rocket—Starship Version 3. Starship and its Super Heavy booster lift off from SpaceX's launch site in South Texas at 5:51 pm CDT on July 24, 2026. Credit: Reginald Mathalone/NurPhoto via Getty Images The 408-foot-tall (124-meter) rocket lifted off from Starbase, Texas, a few miles north of the US-Mexico border, at 5:51 pm CDT (6:51 pm EDT; 22:51 UTC). Thirty-three methane-fueled Raptor engines on the Super Heavy booster steered the rocket east over the Gulf of Mexico and into the upper atmosphere, where the booster separated from Starship's upper stage after burning most of its cryogenic propellant. The only thing left incomplete on SpaceX's checklist for Flight 13 was the controlled splashdown of the Super Heavy booster. It was supposed to relight its engines for a landing burn off the coast of Texas, simulating maneuvers required to return the booster back to the launch pad for recovery and reuse. But some of the Raptor engines failed to restart for the landing burn, and the booster fell into the ocean at high speed. SpaceX also had trouble with the booster splashdown on the last flight in May. Friday's flight showed some progress, but engineers have more work to do on recovering this version the Super Heavy booster. SpaceX previously recovered and re-flew Super Heavy boosters two times with the Starship Version 2 design, but not with Version 3. "The booster successfully completed the high thrust portion of the boostback burn with all 33 engines, the first time with a Super Heavy V3, before ending the burn early," SpaceX officials wrote in an update on the company's website . "It attempted to relight its engines for the landing burn, with a subset successfully igniting before experiencing a hard splashdown in the Gulf." Success in space Starship continued accelerating into space as the Super Heavy booster descended toward the Gulf, firing its six engines more than five minutes before beginning a half-hour coast over the Caribbean Sea, Atlantic Ocean, and South Africa. A few minutes after engine shutdown, Starship opened its payload bay door and started deploying a stack of 20 Starlink satellites. The satellites are the first of SpaceX's upgraded Starlink V3 model, with significant improvements in throughput and power. They are also larger and heavier than Starlink V2s, meaning they will not fit on SpaceX's smaller, workhorse Falcon 9 rocket. Starship released the Starlink V3s using its Pez-like deployer, tossing them overboard through a slit-like opening on the side of the spacecraft. The flat-panel satellites did not stay in space for long. They flew on the same arcing suborbital trajectory as Starship, and were designed to burn up as they fell back into the atmosphere less than an hour after launch. In little time, SpaceX ground teams established contact with each of the satellites through radio and laser communication links, and "downloaded key telemetry" before their fiery demise. This provided engineers with their first look at the performance of Starlink V3s in space. Powered by six Raptor engines, Starship is seen accelerating toward space Friday in this view captured by a camera on the Super Heavy booster moments after stage separation. Credit: SpaceX With the satellite deployments complete, attention turned to a brief restart of one of the ship's Raptor engines, something engineers forewent on the last flight. The burn lasted approximately 14 seconds, and was visible to observers in South Africa. SpaceX hailed the demonstration as "core capability for future orbital missions." Gravity then pulled Starship back to Earth. The next steps for Starship are getting to orbit and returning the ship to the launch site. Those achievements will give SpaceX the capability to begin launching operational Starlink V3 satellites, unlocking higher-speed direct-to-device connectivity for consumers and the US military, and the revenue to go along with it. For NASA, an orbital flight puts SpaceX on a path toward orbital refueling. This demonstration is vital for any Starship flight beyond low-Earth orbit, including missions to the Moon in support of NASA's Artemis program. NASA is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop human-rated versions of Starship and the Blue Moon lander to ferry astronauts to and from the lunar surface. "Excited for what will be learned from this mission," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote on X after the launch of Flight 13. "When Starship comes online, its capabilities will be game-changing, not least of which will be ensuring we never give up the Moon again!" SpaceX has one active launch pad in Texas, and a second Starship pad undergoing renovations there. Two Starship launch sites are under construction at Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The orbital refueling demonstration will include two Starship launches, allowing the vehicles to rendezvous and dock with one another in orbit. One ship will then transfer methane and liquid oxygen propellants to the other through automated couplers. It will take multiple refueling runs in rapid succession to refill a Starship with enough propellant to reach the Moon, requiring rapid reuse of Starships and the Super Heavy boosters at multiple launch pads. With Friday's test flight, SpaceX seems poised to embark on the next phase of Starship's iterative development program. It won't be easy. Read full article Comments ]]>

draft_context.source_title: Hori won me back with its Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2, but some annoying design quirks stop it short of greatness
draft_context.description: Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2: One-minute review The Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2 is far from being one of the best Nintendo Switch 2 controllers , but it gets a lot right, and in my testing I found it to be a solid—if unremarkable—stand-in for the official Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller . After I reviewed the frankly terrible Horipad for Steam , I didn't have high hopes for the Wireless Horipad Turbo. I've been rendered pleasantly surprised, as there is plenty to like about the brand's latest Nintendo-facing controller. There are a decent number of features for the price, and build quality is generally solid. It's just a shame that a few limitations and design quirks stop it short of an outright recommendation. (Image credit: Future) Let's frontload the review with the good, though. Hori has opted for anti-drift thumbsticks that feel great and ensure longevity. That's something the Wireless Horipad Turbo has over the Switch 2 Pro Controller, which utilizes traditional analog sticks and is thus more likely to develop stick drift over time. Build quality is generally nice, too. While larger than the Pro Controller (and thus better suited to big adult hands), it feels solid enough, and a selection of colorways is always really nice to see. I'm a fan of the feature set, too, with the Wireless Horipad Turbo offering a robust Turbo button option, as well as two remappable rear buttons and a button lock switch that disables utility buttons like Start, Select, Home, and Capture (for taking screenshots). There's even a GameChat button for quick access to social gaming sessions. It's a shame, then, that the Wireless Horipad Turbo doesn't quite stick the landing in a few key areas. Battery life is paltry, falling well short of the Switch 2 Pro Controller's 40- to 50-hour gold standard. The d-pad and triggers, specifically, aren't the best—feeling incredibly mushy during play, which really isn't something you want for digital triggers in particular. Lastly, a lack of PC compatibility means this is strictly a Nintendo Switch 2 controller. That's not necessarily a bad thing if that's solely what you're after (and it's likely a result of this being an officially licensed Nintendo product). But it does make it a less versatile controller than the likes of the 8BitDo Pro 3 . (Image credit: Future) Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2: Price and availability Costs $64.99 / £54.99 (around AU$93) Available to buy now at Hori's store page, Amazon, or local retailers Cheaper than the Switch 2 Pro Controller, and offers several colorways The Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2 is available to buy now, and you've got options as to where you purchase it from. You can get it directly from Hori, Amazon, or local retailers based on your region, such as Best Buy in the US and Argos in the UK. It'll run you $64.99 / £54.99 (around AU$93), which is a good deal cheaper than the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller ($89.99 / £74.99 / AU$119.95). You'll also find a healthy amount of colorways to choose from. Hori sent me the standard Black and Frost variants for review, but there's also an Aqua model, as well as special liveries based on Nintendo properties like Kirby and Super Mario. Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2: Specs Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2 Price $64.99 / £54.99 (around AU$93) Weight 8.3oz / 235g Dimensions 5.7 x 4.5 x 2.2in / 145 x 114 x 57mm Compatibility Nintendo Switch 2 Connection type Wireless (Bluetooth) Battery life 10 hours Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2: Design and features Eye-catching translucent design Handy Turbo and button lock features Generally solid build quality One way for a controller to win me over is if it sports a translucent design. It's a style I'm happy to see come in vogue again over the last few years, at least when it comes to controllers, and it helps the Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2 really stand out. I'm a huge fan of the crystal-clear Frost colorway, especially. It doesn't just win out in the looks department, though. Build quality is really solid here; a huge step up from the listless Horipad for Steam, which I reviewed prior to this. It's not as premium as the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller, but the Wireless Horipad Turbo feels really solid and secure in the hands, with just the right amount of weight to it. (Image credit: Future) The titular 'Turbo' feature is niche; not everyone will find a use for it, but it's a nice-to-have for retro games or ones that require frequent, rapid button presses. Holding down the central Hori logo button in tandem with 'A' will then let you assign a button for the Turbo input. You can also press the Start and Select buttons to adjust the speed of the Turbo setting by three increments, too. Another feature I quite like (but again, it is probably quite niche) is the button lock switch. It's off by default, but one setting completely disables the Hori, Home, and Capture buttons, while another turns those off in addition to Start and Select. I know I've accidentally hit the Home button instead of Start more times than I care to admit on the Pro Controller, so this is a thoughtful addition. The button lock switch doesn't extend to the pair of remappable buttons on the rear, but you can just leave these unassigned if you prefer. Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2: Performance Performant TMR thumbsticks Poor battery life Weak-feeling triggers and mushy d-pad Controllers that make use of TMR (that's tunneling magnetoresistance) thumbsticks are a dime a dozen in today's gaming hardware marketplace. It's more common to find them than not now, but this is the first time I've tested a Hori controller with TMR. And I'm glad the brand has opted for them with the Wireless Horipad Turbo. They feel fantastically smooth during play, and as it's a form of Hall effect technology, it should ensure the pad's longevity for years to come. Otherwise, this is a fairly unremarkable but inoffensive controller purely from a play standpoint. It lacks things like HD Rumble, an NFC touchpoint for amiibo scanning, and 'press to wake' functionality for the console itself. However, as these are niceties reserved for Nintendo's own hardware, it's hard to leverage this as a complaint at Hori. The lack of a 3.5mm port for wired headphones does irk me, though, because wireless audio via Bluetooth on Switch 2 is shoddy at best. I'm also not a big fan of the controller's d-pad. It feels rather mushy to press, which at worst can often lead to inputs very occasionally not registering. Much the same is true of the triggers, which are supposed to be digital, but kind of feel like they're made of sponge. Thankfully, connectivity isn't an issue. The controller paired immediately to my Switch 2 console, and I never experienced dropouts or noticeable input delay. And that's for the best, as this is a wireless-first controller. You can still plug in the controller via the included USB-C for charging purposes and carry on playing. And you might be doing that frequently, as the Wireless Horipad Turbo tops out at just 10 hours of charge. That's not much better than PlayStation's DualSense Wireless Controller , and falls well short of the Switch 2 Pro Controller's monster 40-hour battery life. Lastly, it is unfortunate that the Wireless Horipad Turbo can't be used for PC gaming. The Switch 2 Pro Controller can't either, so I suspect this is a Nintendo-issued requirement, as the Turbo bears the company's seal of approval. It just means that it's not as versatile as third-party pads from the likes of 8BitDo and GameSir. (Image credit: Future) Should I buy the Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2? Buy it if… You want a performant Switch 2 controller that's built to last TMR sticks will ensure this controller's longevity, and as a result, it shouldn't fall victim to stick drift even after months or years of usage. You don't have the budget for a Switch 2 Pro Controller The Wireless Horipad Turbo is significantly cheaper than the console's official gamepad option. And with nice colorways and some neat features, it's really not a bad fallback option. Don’t buy it if… You want beefier battery life At just 10 hours of charge, you'll be topping this thing up very frequently if you regularly play your Switch or Switch 2 in docked mode. You want something multiplatform If you like to game on multiple devices away from your Switch or Switch 2 (like PC or mobile), you might want to look elsewhere as this is strictly a Nintendo-facing pad. Also consider... If the Wireless Horipad Turbo has a few too many issues for your liking, consider the following alternatives. Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2 Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller 8BitDo Pro 3 Price $64.99 / £54.99 (around AU$93) $89.99 / £74.99 / AU$119.95 $59.99 / £40 (around AU$84) Weight 8.3oz / 235g 8.3oz / 235g 8.5oz / 242g Dimensions 5.7 x 4.5 x 2.2in / 145 x 114 x 57mm 5.8 x 4.1 x 2.4in / 148 x 105 x 60mm 6.1 x 3.9 x 2.6in / 154 x 101 x 65mm Compatibility Switch 2, Switch Switch 2 Switch, Switch 2, PC, iOS, Android Connection type Wireless (Bluetooth) Wireless (Bluetooth), Wired (USB Type-C) Wireless (2.4GHz, Bluetooth), Wired (USB-C) Battery life 10 hours Around 40 hours 15-20 hours Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller Still the premium standard on Switch 2 more than a year on from release. And it's little wonder; Nintendo's official pad has a luxurious feel, and is stuffed with features including HD Rumble, NFC, remappable buttons, and enviable battery life. Read our full Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller review 8BitDo Pro 3 My favorite Nintendo Switch 2 controller, and one that's very hard to argue with at its budget-friendly price point. Honestly, it does everything the Wireless Horipad Turbo does, but better, and more besides. Read our full 8BitDo Pro 3 review How I tested the Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2 Tested for one week Tested on Nintendo Switch 2 with a variety of modern and retro titles Used features like the Turbo functionality and button lock switch For this review, I tested the Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2 on the console of the same name for about a week. I played a good mix of modern and old-school titles with the controller, including Star Fox , Street Fighter 6 , Rhythm Heaven Groove , as well as Ridge Racer 64 and Super Mario 64 via Nintendo Switch Online's N64 library. During testing, I made use of the Turbo functionality to enable easier, rapid button presses in classic titles like Metal Slug 3. Meanwhile, I went back and forth with the button lock switch, and I can confidently say it stopped me from accidentally backing out to the Home dashboard on a few occasions. I'd love to see this feature make a comeback for future Hori products. Read more about how we test First reviewed July 2026 ]]>
paragraphs: (Image credit: © Future) TechRadar Verdict If you need a spare Switch 2 controller, or you don't feel like paying for the expensive official Switch 2 Pro Controller, then the Wireless Horipad Turbo is a decent stand-in. Anti-drift TMR sticks are a plus over the Pro Controller, and the robust Turbo feature is great for arcade and retro games. I'm just not huge on some elements like the mushy-feeling d-pad and triggers, and a lack of PC compatibility means that multiplatform use is strictly off the table.
Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.

Jump To: One-minute review Price and availability Specs Design and features Performance How I tested Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2: One-minute review The Wireless Horipad Turbo for Nintendo Switch 2 is far from being one of the best Nintendo Switch 2 controllers , but it gets a lot right, and in my testing I found it to be a solid—if unremarkable—stand-in for the official Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller .

After I reviewed the frankly terrible Horipad for Steam , I didn't have high hopes for the Wireless Horipad Turbo. I've been rendered pleasantly surprised, as there is plenty to like about the brand's latest Nintendo-facing controller. There are a decent number of features for the price, and build quality is generally solid. It's just a shame that a few limitations and design quirks stop it short of an outright recommendation.

Let's frontload the review with the good, though. Hori has opted for anti-drift thumbsticks that feel great and ensure longevity. That's something the Wireless Horipad Turbo has over the Switch 2 Pro Controller, which utilizes traditional analog sticks and is thus more likely to develop stick drift over time.

articles.title: Hà Nội khai mạc Hội nghị KOL & ra mắt CLB Niềm tin số Thủ đô
articles.summary: Chiều ngày 24/7/2026, Hội nghị KOL và Lễ ra mắt Câu lạc bộ (CLB) Niềm tin số Thủ đô chính thức diễn ra tại Hà Nội với thông điệp "Trọn niềm tin số - Kiến tạo tương lai". Tín hiệu từ GenK Tin ICT cần được đặt vào bối cảnh trước: thời điểm xuất hiện, chi tiết đã có cơ sở và lý do nó đáng nằm trong dòng tin công nghệ hôm nay.

sections.heading: Bối cảnh: điều gì vừa đổi
sections.body: Chiều ngày 24/7/2026, Hội nghị KOL và Lễ ra mắt Câu lạc bộ (CLB) Niềm tin số Thủ đô chính thức diễn ra tại Hà Nội với thông điệp "Trọn niềm tin số - Kiến tạo tương lai". Tín hiệu từ GenK Tin ICT cần được đặt vào bối cảnh trước: thời điểm xuất hiện, chi tiết đã có cơ sở và lý do nó đáng nằm trong dòng tin công nghệ hôm nay. Phần này cần dựng lại thay đổi đã có cơ sở trước khi chuyển sang nhận định.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Chương trình mở đầu bằng các tiết mục trình diễn đến từ nhiều nghệ sĩ như Hà Myo, Tuấn Cry, Ngô Lan Hương,. Tiếp sau đó là giới thiệu đại biểu, lãnh đạo các cơ quan quản lý cùng những đơn vị đồng hành tham dự, phiên tọa đàm, khen thưởng, đồng thời công bố mục tiêu, sứ mệnh và tầm nhìn của CLB Niềm tin số Thủ đô trong giai đoạn đầu hoạt động. Tác động thực tế nằm ở workflow, chi phí, rủi ro hoặc quyết định mua/dùng; Hà Nội khai mạc Hội nghị KOL & ra mắt CLB Niềm tin số Thủ đô nên được giải thích qua lăng kính đó trước khi kết luận rộng hơn. Phần này cần nối câu chuyện với workflow, chi phí, bảo mật hoặc quyết định dùng/mua của người đọc.

sections.heading: Chi tiết cần kiểm chứng
sections.body: Hội nghị ghi nhận sự tham dự của các đồng chí lãnh đạo đại diện các bộ, ngành Trung ương: Đại tá, NSND Vũ Tự Long, Giám đốc Nhà hát Chèo Quân đội; NSND Xuân Bắc, Cục trưởng Cục Nghệ thuật Biểu diễn, Bộ Văn hoá, Thể thao và Du lịch; ông Trịnh Anh Tuấn, Chủ tịch Ủy ban Cạnh tranh Quốc gia; bà Nguyễn Thị Thanh Huyền, Phó Cục trưởng Cục Phát thanh, Truyền hình và Thông tin điện tử. Câu hỏi tiếp theo là tín hiệu này có thành rollout bền vững, thay đổi giá trị sản phẩm, giới hạn đáng chú ý hay chỉ là một nhịp cập nhật ngắn. Phần này chỉ giữ chi tiết có thể kiểm chứng và tránh lặp lại nguyên văn cách diễn đạt của nguồn.

sections.heading: Ai nên hành động hoặc chờ
sections.body: Sự kiện còn có sự tham dự của ông Trương Việt Dũng, Phó Chủ tịch UBND TP Hà Nội, lãnh đạo các sở, ngành cùng lực lượng Công an và cộng đồng những người có sức ảnh hưởng trên không gian mạng (KOL), doanh nghiệp truyền thông lớn. Với người đọc, khung hữu ích gồm bằng chứng hiện có, nhóm bị ảnh hưởng, rủi ro còn lại và điểm nên kiểm tra trước khi hành động. Phần này cần gọi đúng nhóm độc giả nên hành động ngay hoặc nên chờ thêm xác nhận.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Trung tướng Nguyễn Thanh Tùng, Anh hùng lực lượng vũ trang nhân dân, Ủy viên Ban Thường vụ Thành ủy, Bí thư Đảng ủy, Giám đốc CATP Hà Nội đã cùng thực hiện nghi thức ra mắt và tặng hoa chúc mừng lãnh đạo Câu lạc bộ. Một bài tốt cần tách rõ sự kiện từ nguồn, tác động với người đọc và câu hỏi theo dõi để không giống bản tóm tắt link rời. Phần này nên khép lại bằng tín hiệu cần kiểm tra tiếp, không tóm tắt lại cùng một ý.
